metadata.note: Authored by Claude from the panel schema during development (no API key in the environment); regenerate live with `python scripts/run_analysis.py --live`. LLM proposals are advisory; Python computes all statistics. Hashes bind this artifact to the exact panel schema context and gate it was written against; a mismatched replay is rejected as stale.

avg_food_desert_pct.description: population-weighted share of residents in food-desert tracts, 0-1 scale

dac_tract_pct.description: share of tracts flagged as disadvantaged communities

med_household_income.description: median household income, $ (NCCS/ACS) -- an INVERSE-need/context measure: high income = low need

ngo_per_10k.description: registered nonprofits per 10k residents (ordered, truncated ~1M-row NGO extract)

food_ngo_per_10k.description: 'Food, Agriculture and Nutrition' nonprofits per 10k residents

revenue_per_capita.description: 990/990EZ/990PF-filer total revenue per capita, $ (sparse ~3.6% filer match; NaN where no filer)

assets_per_capita.description: 990/990EZ/990PF-filer net assets per capita, $ (sparse ~3.6% filer match; NaN where no filer)

candidates.hypothesis: Counties with larger food-desert shares are underserved by food-focused nonprofits per capita, since food NGOs cluster where donors and infrastructure exist rather than where food access is worst.
High-poverty counties support fewer nonprofits per 10k residents because organizational density follows local wealth, philanthropy, and professional capacity.
Wealthier counties host better-funded nonprofits, so median household income should track filer revenue per capita.
Nonprofit financial resources per resident thin out in poor counties, mirroring the income relationship from the opposite direction.
Counties with high unemployment have weaker civic infrastructure and therefore fewer registered nonprofits per capita.
Housing-cost burden concentrates in expensive metro counties that also host asset-rich institutions, so burden may correlate positively with nonprofit assets per capita.
Counties with more disadvantaged-community tracts attract targeted food programming, but per-capita presence likely still lags, on net negative.

gate_review.rationale: Need-side tables and joins are all usable, so the panel's denominators are sound. On the full 3,420,024-row table the capacity-side drop is now almost entirely Florida and Connecticut, whose counties are unmappable in the committed lookup; that absence is logged, non-fatal, and must stay disclosed in any national claim.

proposal.narrative_notes: Frame the gap score as a triage map, not a performance ranking: high-gap counties are places worth investigating, not evidence that local nonprofits underperform. Lead with the geography of the top-gap counties, then use the correlation grid to show that capacity tracks wealth rather than need. Note that the analysis now runs on the full table rather than the truncated extract, with Virginia's independent cities recovered by the exact-first crosswalk. Flag the sparse 990 filer join wherever financial metrics appear, and keep Florida and Connecticut's lookup-driven absence visible in every county count.
